explanations.explanation: Verse 2 says it plainly: the Spirit of God came upon Azariah son of Oded, so he went out to meet Asa, Judah's king. Out to meet Asa is exactly where he goes. And then he says, “Listen to me, Asa and all Judah and Benjamin.”
Praying in the temple sounds like a good plan, but it isn't what the text says. It says Azariah went out to meet Asa. When he speaks, he says, “Listen to me, Asa and all Judah and Benjamin.”

The hill country does show up in this passage, but later. Verse 8 mentions the cities Asa had captured in the hill country of Ephraim. In verse 2, though, Azariah goes out to meet Asa. Good guess, friend, but that's a different part of the story.

That's it. Azariah says, “The LORD is with you when you are with Him.” Notice it's not about what Judah has, but about being with Him. That's the whole sentence, and it's a good one to hang on the fridge.

Strength is the first thing a lot of us think of, so I get the pick. But Azariah never says the LORD is with them when their army is strong. He says, “The LORD is with you when you are with Him.” The thing that matters is being with Him.

Winning feels like proof of everything, doesn't it? But Azariah doesn't tie the LORD being with them to a win. He says, “The LORD is with you when you are with Him.” Being with Him is the thing, and the scoreboard isn't mentioned.

It goes the other way, friend. Azariah says, “If you seek Him, He will be found by you, but if you forsake Him, He will forsake you.” So the promise has two sides, and he says both out loud. That's a message with no small print.
Right. Azariah says, “If you seek Him, He will be found by you, but if you forsake Him, He will forsake you.” Two roads, both clearly marked. I like a sign that tells you the truth up front.

explanations.answer: They sought the LORD and found Him
explanations.explanation: Verse 4 says, “But in their distress they turned to the LORD, the God of Israel, and sought Him, and He was found by them.” They turned to the LORD in their distress, and He was found by them. That's exactly what Azariah promised in verse 2.

explanations.answer: They looked to other nations for help
explanations.explanation: Looking around for help is a very human move when things get hard. But that's not what Azariah says Israel did. He says they turned to the LORD, the God of Israel, and sought Him.

explanations.answer: They made new idols for protection
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that about this moment. Azariah says that in their distress they turned to the LORD, the God of Israel, and sought Him. And He was found by them.

It's right there in verse 6: “…for God afflicted them with all kinds of adversity.” It comes right after nation was crushed by nation, and city by city. This is one of the heavy parts of Azariah's message, so it deserves a quiet moment.
Verse 6 says it outright: “…for God afflicted them with all kinds of adversity.” That's after nation was crushed by nation, and city by city. It's a heavy line, and it really is in the text.

Yes, courage. Verse 8 says, “When Asa heard these words and the prophecy of Azariah son of Oded the prophet, he took courage…” Azariah told him to be strong, and Asa took it to heart. And then he got busy.
Some of us take offense when somebody has a hard word for us, and I've done it myself. But that isn't what Asa did. Verse 8 says he took courage.
Asa did hear the prophecy, so I see where this comes from. But verse 8 says what he took from it: “…he took courage…” Azariah had just told him, “…be strong; do not be discouraged…”

Idols is right. Verse 8 says Asa “…removed the detestable idols from the whole land of Judah and Benjamin…” He also removed them from the cities he had captured in the hill country of Ephraim. Courage went straight to work.
No beasts here, friend. Verse 8 says Asa “…removed the detestable idols from the whole land of Judah and Benjamin…” It's the idols that go.
Ruins isn't what's in verse 8. It says Asa “…removed the detestable idols from the whole land of Judah and Benjamin…” This is clearing out, and no tearing down a building is mentioned.

Yes. Verse 8 says, “He then restored the altar of the LORD that was in front of the portico of the LORD’s temple.” First the idols go out, then the altar is set right. Asa cleans the house and fixes what matters.

The ark is a holy thing, but it doesn't come up in this passage. Verse 8 says, “He then restored the altar of the LORD that was in front of the portico of the LORD’s temple.” So the altar is what Asa restored.
The bronze Sea isn't mentioned in this passage. Verse 8 names what Asa restored: “…the altar of the LORD that was in front of the portico of the LORD’s temple.” That's the one.

Verse 9 says so: “…for great numbers had come over to him from Israel when they saw that the LORD his God was with him.” They saw that the LORD his God was with him, and they came. Verse 9 also says Asa assembled all Judah and Benjamin, along with those from the tribes of Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon who had settled among them.
It's true, friend. Verse 9 says “…great numbers had come over to him from Israel when they saw that the LORD his God was with him.” Quite a crowd, and the text tells us why they came.

Verse 11 says they sacrificed the seven hundred oxen and seven thousand sheep “…from all the plunder they had brought back.” Those numbers aren't small. And it shows what they did with what they carried home.
Asa is king, so it's a fair guess. But verse 11 doesn't say the animals came from his herds. It says they came from all the plunder they had brought back.
The text doesn't point to the priests' fields. Verse 11 says the animals came “…from all the plunder they had brought back.” That's the source it gives.

explanations.answer: With all their heart and soul
explanations.explanation: Verse 12 says they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, “…with all their heart and soul.” That's all in, nothing held back. It matches what Azariah told them about seeking Him.
They had just made a big offering, so I see why this one tempts. But the covenant in verse 12 doesn't mention feasts. They agree to seek the LORD “…with all their heart and soul.”

Fasting and sackcloth aren't mentioned in this passage. Verse 12 says they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, “…with all their heart and soul.” That's how they say they'll seek Him.

explanations.answer: They would be put to death
explanations.explanation: Verse 13 says, “…whoever would not seek the LORD, the God of Israel, would be put to death…” That's a heavy line, and I won't pretend it isn't. It shows how seriously they took the covenant they had just made.

explanations.answer: They would be sent out of Judah
explanations.explanation: Verse 13 doesn't say that. It says, “…whoever would not seek the LORD, the God of Israel, would be put to death…” It's a heavy part of the passage, and the text states it plainly.

explanations.answer: They would pay a fine to the priests
explanations.explanation: No fine is mentioned. Verse 13 says, “…whoever would not seek the LORD, the God of Israel, would be put to death…” It's a heavy line, and it's what the text says.

Verse 13 closes that door. It says whoever would not seek the LORD, the God of Israel, would be put to death, “…whether young or old, man or woman.” The text doesn't limit it to the men of Judah, so women are named right in the verse.

Right. Verse 13 says whoever would not seek the LORD, the God of Israel, would be put to death, “…whether young or old, man or woman.” The text doesn't limit it to the men. It's a heavy verse, but the wording is clear.

Verse 15 says, “And all Judah rejoiced over the oath, for they had sworn it with all their heart.” After the shouting, trumpets and rams' horns, joy fits. And it says all Judah, so nobody was sitting this one out.
An oath that serious could make anyone's knees knock. But verse 15 says, “And all Judah rejoiced over the oath…” They had sworn it with all their heart, and it shows in their joy.
Weeping isn't mentioned in this passage. Verse 15 says all Judah rejoiced over the oath, for they had sworn it with all their heart. Rejoiced is the word the text gives.
Yes. Verse 15 says, “So the LORD gave them rest on every side.” They sought Him earnestly, and He was found by them, just like Azariah said. Rest on every side is a gift any of us could use.
A temple would be a big gift, but the text doesn't say He gave one here. Verse 15 says, “So the LORD gave them rest on every side.” Rest is what the text says He gave them.
Egypt doesn't come up in this passage. Verse 15 says, “So the LORD gave them rest on every side.” Rest on every side is the gift the text names.

The text doesn't say that. Verse 16 says Asa removed Maacah, his grandmother, from her position as queen mother “…because she had made a detestable Asherah pole.” A plot for the throne isn't mentioned.

Right. Verse 16 says Asa removed Maacah, his grandmother, from her position as queen mother “…because she had made a detestable Asherah pole.” No plot is mentioned. I think that was a hard thing for a king to do in his own family.
Half of it is right. Asa did clear out idols, and verse 8 says so. But verse 17 says, “The high places were not removed from Israel…” So this statement goes too far.

Right. Asa did clear idols out, but verse 17 says, “The high places were not removed from Israel…” The text gives us both parts, the good work and what was left standing. So saying the high places were removed doesn't match the text.
Verse 17 says, “…Asa’s heart was fully devoted all his days.” The high places were still standing, and the text tells us this about his heart anyway. It's one sentence, and it's a lovely one.
Two paths? Not for Asa's heart, friend. Verse 17 says, “…Asa’s heart was fully devoted all his days.” That's the description the text gives, and divided isn't in it.

Proud? I get the guess, friend, but the text doesn't describe his heart that way. Verse 17 says, “…Asa’s heart was fully devoted all his days.” Devoted is the word it uses, and it says for how long: all his days.
Yes. Verse 19 says, “And there was no war until the thirty-fifth year of Asa’s reign.” Quiet right up until that year of his reign. That's a lot of peaceful batches.
The twentieth year isn't the one. Verse 19 says there was no war until the thirty-fifth year of Asa's reign. So the twentieth falls short of the number the text gives.
Close, but too far down the road. Verse 19 says there was no war until the thirty-fifth year of Asa's reign. The text gives that number, and it stops there.
